page: Amazon Web Services i2.4xlarge is a storage-optimized virtual machine instance running on the Xen hypervisor. It features an x86_64 architecture powered by an Intel Xeon E5-2670 v2 processor with 16 vCPUs and 8 physical cores. The CPU operates at 2.5 GHz and includes a 25 MB L3 cache. The instance is equipped with 122.0 GB of system memory, providing 7.62 GB per core. For local storage, it bundles 3200 GB of NVMe SSD capacity. Network performance is defined by a baseline bandwidth of 2 Gbps.

Performance benchmarks show average results across several compute and memory metrics, alongside notable bottlenecks. The instance achieves average ratings in stress-ng single-core and multi-core tests, as well as PassMark CPU and database operations. However, single-threaded performance is a weakness, with Geekbench single-core scoring in the bottom 10% and bzip3 single-threaded decompression also rating poor. Memory read bandwidth is strong at 588.91 GB/sec for cached small blocks, but large block write bandwidth drops to a weak 18.74 GB/sec.

From a qualitative cost-efficiency perspective, the i2.4xlarge offers high local NVMe storage density and substantial memory capacity relative to its legacy Intel hardware class. However, the older CPU architecture limits its performance-per-resource efficiency for modern compute-heavy tasks, as evidenced by weak multi-core Geekbench scores and low LLM inference speeds. This instance is best suited for storage-intensive workloads, database operations, and static web serving that benefit from large local SSD capacity and moderate memory, rather than raw CPU-bound processing or modern machine learning tasks.
description: Amazon Web Services i2.4xlarge is a storage-optimized instance utilizing the Xen hypervisor and x86_64 architecture. It is configured with an Intel Xeon E5-2670 v2 processor offering 16 vCPUs, 8 physical cores, and a 2.5 GHz clock speed. The hardware profile includes 122.0 GB of RAM and a bundled 3200 GB NVMe SSD for high-capacity local storage, supported by a 2 Gbps baseline network bandwidth. Benchmark data indicates average performance in multi-core CPU tests and database operations, though single-core execution and memory write speeds are relatively weak. Qualitatively, the instance provides high local storage density, making it a viable option for legacy database hosting, static web serving, and storage-heavy applications. However, its older processor architecture makes it less efficient for modern compute-intensive workloads or machine learning inference.
